source: original; documents are public-domain primary sources or paraphrases of them (see each document's sourcing note)
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which Jefferson's presidency changed American politics, 1800-1812.

documents.title: Jefferson's First Inaugural Address
documents.source: Thomas Jefferson, First Inaugural Address, March 4, 1801, abridged. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Jefferson speaking to a divided country days after winning the bitter election of 1800.
documents.text: “We have called by different names brethren of the same principle. We are all Republicans, we are all Federalists. … peace, commerce, and honest friendship with all nations, entangling alliances with none; the support of the State governments in all their rights, as the most competent administrations for our domestic concerns.”

documents.title: Federalist warnings against Jefferson
documents.source: Federalist newspaper warnings during the campaign of 1800, paraphrased. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Federalist writers trying to frighten voters away from Jefferson in a bitter campaign.
documents.text: Federalist writers warned that Jefferson's election would bring the terror of the French Revolution to American shores. They called him a danger to religion and order.

documents.title: Marshall on the duty of the courts
documents.source: Chief Justice John Marshall, Marbury v. Madison (1803), abridged. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Marshall writing the Court's opinion in a case about an undelivered judicial commission.
documents.text: “It is emphatically the province and duty of the judicial department to say what the law is. Those who apply the rule to particular cases, must of necessity expound and interpret that rule.”

documents.title: Jefferson doubts the Louisiana Purchase
documents.source: Thomas Jefferson to John Breckinridge, August 12, 1803, abridged. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Jefferson writing privately to a fellow Republican about the constitutional problem of the purchase.
documents.text: “The constitution has made no provision for our holding foreign territory, still less for incorporating foreign nations into our Union. The Executive in seizing the fugitive occurrence which so much advances the good of their country, have done an act beyond the Constitution.”

documents.title: The Twelfth Amendment
documents.source: Twelfth Amendment to the Constitution, proposed 1803, ratified 1804, abridged. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The amendment written to fix the electoral tie of 1800.
documents.text: “The Electors shall meet in their respective states and vote by ballot for President and Vice-President, one of whom, at least, shall not be an inhabitant of the same state with themselves; they shall name in their ballots the person voted for as President, and in distinct ballots the person voted for as Vice-President.”

documents.title: Ograbme, the American snapping-turtle
documents.source: American cartoon, 1807-1808. Public domain; image from the shared image pool.
documents.sourcing: A cartoonist mocking Jefferson's Embargo Act while American ports stood idle.

documents.title: Presidential elections, 1800-1808
documents.source: Electoral vote totals from the National Archives.
documents.sourcing: Election returns showing the Democratic-Republicans' growing hold on the presidency.
documents.text:
| Election | Winner | Electoral votes | Runner-up | Electoral votes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1800 | Thomas Jefferson | 73 | Aaron Burr | 73 |
| 1804 | Thomas Jefferson | 162 | Charles C. Pinckney | 14 |
| 1808 | James Madison | 122 | Charles C. Pinckney | 47 |

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which Jefferson's presidency changed American politics, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of change does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the party battles of the 1790s, the new republic's fragile institutions, or the Napoleonic Wars in Europe.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing the content of at least three documents relevant to the argument, such as Jefferson's inaugural, the Marbury opinion, or the election table.
rubric.notEarned: Quoting documents without describing what they show does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support the argument, including documents that show the limits of change.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or using six without tying them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific relevant example not in the documents, such as Jefferson's repeal of the whiskey tax, his keeping of the national bank, or the Burr-Hamilton duel of 1804.
rubric.notEarned: A vague reference to outside knowledge with no specific example does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining how the audience, purpose, historical situation, or point of view of at least two documents shapes the argument, such as Jefferson writing privately to Breckinridge, or the cartoonist mocking the embargo for a port-city audience.
rubric.notEarned: Naming a document's author without explaining how it shapes the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for a complex argument, such as qualifying the thesis by showing where Jefferson changed politics and where older structures survived, or weighing the peaceful transfer of power against the persistence of party conflict.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: Jefferson's presidency changed American politics profoundly but not completely: it proved power could pass peacefully between parties and stretched the presidency beyond its old limits, yet it left the Federalist program alive in the courts and the party system itself intact.
Context: The 1790s had been a decade of bitter party war, with the Alien and Sedition Acts jailing critics and both sides calling the other a danger to the republic. The election of 1800 was the first test of whether a loser would hand over power.
Evidence of change: Document 1 shows Jefferson calming the losers and preaching limited government. Document 5 shows the system learning from its own failure, with separate ballots for president and vice president. Document 7 shows the result: Jefferson wins 162 votes to 14 in 1804, and Madison follows him in 1808.
Evidence of limits: Document 3 shows the Federalist program surviving in the Marshall Court, which claimed the power to void laws. Document 4 shows Jefferson himself breaking his own strict construction to buy Louisiana. Document 6 shows his embargo failing at home, biting Americans instead of Britain and France.
Beyond the documents: Jefferson repealed the whiskey tax and let the Alien and Sedition Acts lapse, yet he kept Hamilton's bank, a Federalist institution he had once opposed.
Sourcing: Jefferson writes privately to Breckinridge about doubts he would never voice in public, while the cartoonist draws for merchants whose livelihoods the embargo destroyed.
Complexity: The presidency changed hands peacefully and grew stronger, but the change was uneven: the parties, the courts, and the Constitution's gaps all survived Jefferson's revolution, and his own presidency proved that principles bend when opportunity calls.
